items.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: So now he says, “Who can we send to New York, to make one of these mainstream jazz?” So I’d just sold a business of my father’s and I was kind of free, and I said well I could go.

ctx.x: The Ellington of that time, of the ‘30s, he was really doing something very new. Do you think people responded to the swing part of his music, or was it the compositions themselves that really were very new?

Well it was — I mean he had a much more varied program or book than the other bands. There was everything they had really. Certainly it was superior, and he had very excellent soloists. But of course what Helen was mostly doing was they were recording — Irving Mills had two labels, one a regular price, like Victor or Columbia, and the other one, Variety, was a cheaper one, thirty-five cents I think at retail. And they were recording all small units of Duke’s bands and other small bands that she put together. And…
And you said they were LPs? They weren’t ten inch records? They were —
